To hassle someone means to repeatedly bother, pressure, or annoy them — often to make them do something they aren't doing, or simply because you want something from them and you won't leave them alone until you get it.

Three things together make an action a "hassle":

1. It is repeated or persistent.
It isn't a single complaint or one polite request. The person keeps coming back, keeps pushing, keeps nagging. They don't stop even after you've heard them the first time.

2. It is unwanted.
The person being hassled does not want this attention, pressure, or interference. They find it irritating or stressful.

3. There is pressure behind it.
The person doing the hassling is usually trying to get a response, an action, or compliance. There's a "do what I want" energy behind it — even if it isn't said out loud.

• "My little brother keeps hassling me to let him play on my phone."

→ He's asking again and again, and it's getting annoying.

  • "Stop hassling me! I told you I'll do it later."

→ Someone is pushing the speaker repeatedly and the speaker is fed up.

  • "The sales agent at the store was hassling every customer who walked in."

→ He was pressuring or pestering customers aggressively, making them uncomfortable.

  • "She said her landlord was hassling her about the rent even though she had paid it."

→ The landlord kept bringing it up, pressuring her, even when there was no real reason to.

  • "Don't hassle him — he's having a hard enough day as it is."

→ Don't add to his stress by pressuring or nagging him.
The Two Sides of the Experience

From the hassler's side:
They believe they have a reason to keep pushing. Maybe they feel ignored, or they want something urgently, or they think repeated pressure will finally get a result.

From the hassled person's side:
It feels exhausting, invasive, and frustrating. They feel like they can't get peace. There is a sense of "Why won't you just leave me alone?"

This word appears in many everyday situations:

  • A parent hassling a teenager about their homework or chores
  • An employer hassling an employee about a deadline, repeatedly checking in with impatience
  • A creditor hassling someone about an unpaid bill
  • A friend hassling you to come to a party when you've already said no
  • A person in authority (such as police or security) hassling ordinary people unfairly — in this use, the word carries a sense of injustice and mistreatment
  • A salesperson hassling a customer who is clearly not interested
The Tone and Feel of the Word

"Hassle" is an informal word. You'll hear it in everyday conversation, not in formal writing or official documents. It is direct and slightly sharp — the moment someone says "stop hassling me," there's an edge to it. It signals real annoyance or frustration.

The word belongs to a family of similar words — like pester, nag, bother, badger — but "hassle" has its own specific feel. It tends to carry a slightly heavier sense of persistent pressure than, say, "bother" (which can be a single interruption), but it is usually less severe or threatening than "harass" (which implies a more serious, sustained, and often abusive pattern of behavior). That said, in some contexts — especially when a person in power targets someone unfairly and repeatedly — "hassle" and "harass" can be used to describe very similar behavior.

"Hassle" as a verb always needs an object — you hassle someone. It doesn't work without it.

  • ✅ "She's hassling me."
  • ✅ "He hassled his coworker all week."
  • ✅ "Don't hassle them."
  • ❌ "She's hassling." (incomplete — hassling whom?)
To hassle someone is to repeatedly bother or pressure them in an annoying, persistent way — especially to get them to do something — and to keep doing it even when they clearly don't want you to.
